text: **Middle-ear status before surgery**: active acute otitis media is a contraindication, because the opening into the cochlea gives middle-ear bacteria a route to the inner ear and meninges. Treat it and reschedule once the ear has been free of infection for at least about 2 weeks; children with recurrent otitis media or persistent effusion are often given tympanostomy tubes first and implanted once the ear is dry and stable. Confirm age-appropriate pneumococcal vaccination, ideally completed at least 2 weeks before surgery.

**Fluid found in the middle ear at surgery**: a clear, nonpurulent (serous) effusion with quiet mucosa does not stop the operation. Irrigate the middle ear with saline before opening the cochlea and give topical drops and postoperative antibiotics; series of children implanted with an effusion show more intraoperative difficulty but no increase in postoperative complications, and delaying implantation costs auditory development. Purulent fluid with inflamed mucosa is acute otitis media: do not open the cochlea; culture, place a tympanostomy tube, treat, and implant after at least about 2 weeks free of infection.

**Hearing prognosis on observation**: word recognition (speech discrimination) at diagnosis is the best predictor of long-term serviceable hearing. In the Danish wait-and-scan cohort (Stangerup 2010), 69% of patients with 100% speech discrimination at diagnosis kept good hearing after more than 10 years of observation, compared with 38% of those with even a small discrimination loss. Tumor size, intracanalicular location and age have not consistently predicted hearing outcome, and hearing can decline without tumor growth, so follow audiograms as well as MRI and revisit the treatment discussion if word recognition falls.

**Oral hairy leukoplakia**: white, corrugated, vertically ridged plaques on the lateral borders of the tongue, often on both sides, that cannot be scraped off and do not respond to antifungals. It is caused by Epstein-Barr virus replication in the epithelium and almost always signals systemic immunosuppression: HIV most often, but also transplant immunosuppression, chemotherapy or steroids.

**Confirming oral hairy leukoplakia**: biopsy shows hyperparakeratosis with ballooned, koilocyte-like cells and little inflammation; in situ hybridization for EBV (EBER) confirms the diagnosis. A confirmed case should prompt HIV testing and a search for another cause of immunosuppression if HIV is negative. The lesion is not premalignant and needs no specific treatment; it usually regresses with antiretroviral therapy or restored immunity.

**Oral hairy leukoplakia**: corrugated white plaques on the lateral tongue that do not scrape off, caused by Epstein-Barr virus and almost always a marker of immunosuppression (most often HIV). Confirm with biopsy and EBV in situ hybridization, test for HIV, and expect regression with antiretroviral therapy; it is not premalignant.

**Killian-Jamieson diverticulum**: a less common pouch that arises from the anterolateral wall of the cervical esophagus just below the cricopharyngeus, lateral to the longitudinal esophageal muscle, through the Killian-Jamieson space, often on the left. It lies close to where the recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx. On esophagram it projects laterally below the cricopharyngeal bar, whereas a Zenker pouch arises in the posterior midline above it.

**Killian-Jamieson pouch**: endoscopic stapling of a common wall, the standard for Zenker, risks the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which runs near the pouch neck, so the traditional approach is transcervical diverticulectomy with identification and protection of the nerve (with or without a limited myotomy). Small asymptomatic pouches can be observed. Endoscopic division has been reported in selected cases at experienced centers, but it is not the default, and the nerve's proximity is the reason.
